title: h and chi Persei
caption: The Double Cluster, h and chi Persei, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
celestial: chi Persei, h Persei, NGC 869, NGC 884 · constellation Perseus

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Two star clusters sit side by side in this colour picture. On the left is chi Persei, also called NGC 884, and beside it is h Persei, or NGC 869. Together they form the Double Cluster in the constellation Perseus, usually known by these transliterated Greek labels.

The pair lies about 7000 light-years from us, and the two clusters are less than 100 light-years apart. Open clusters, loose groups of stars born together, are quite common, but this pair is exceptional.

What sets it apart is how many young, bright O and B stars each cluster holds. These are the hottest and most massive kinds of stars, which burn through their fuel quickly and so do not last long; seeing so many of them marks both clusters as young. The two are also unusual for being so close together while still clearly separate.
scale: The two clusters are about 7000 light-years away and less than 100 light-years apart, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak recorded the Double Cluster in visible light, combined into a colour picture; the colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye, revealing many more faint stars and recording their colours.
